main.title: Goof Troop
main.subtitle: A fishing trip interrupted by pirates
main.summary: Goof Troop is Capcom’s 1993 Super Nintendo action-puzzle adventure starring Goofy and his son Max.

cards.heading: A fishing trip interrupted by pirates
cards.text: Goof Troop is Capcom’s 1993 Super Nintendo action-puzzle adventure starring Goofy and his son Max. A fishing trip goes wrong when pirates kidnap Pete and PJ, taking them to Spoonerville Island. Goofy and Max follow them through beaches, jungle paths and a pirate stronghold. The overhead viewpoint makes each room a small arrangement of enemies, obstacles and useful objects rather than a conventional side-scrolling stage. Barrels and pots become improvised weapons, while keys, planks and a grappling tool provide ways through the island. It can be played alone or with a second player controlling the other member of the pair.

cards.heading: Thinking together, one room at a time
cards.text: Progress often depends on changing a room rather than defeating everyone inside it. Kicked blocks slide onto marked squares to open gates, and a mistaken puzzle can be reset by leaving the screen and returning. The manual places its before-and-after examples beside the controls, emphasizing a game of observation and experiment. Goofy is stronger and can defeat some large pirates with a single barrel; Max moves more quickly, giving the partners different strengths. Working together means sharing tools, finding safe positions and leaving space for the other player’s next move. Yuki Iwai, credited under the name Yuki Satomura, composed the music. The result turns the television characters’ family relationship into a cooperative journey built from small, practical problems.

main.title: PC Gamer
main.subtitle: Reviews, cover discs and the culture of PC gaming
main.summary: Future launched PC Gamer in the United Kingdom in 1993. Its American edition followed in June 1994, joining reviews with hardware, demos and the wider life of PC games.

cards.heading: A magazine devoted to the PC
cards.text: PC Gamer began in the United Kingdom in 1993, published by Future. An American sister edition followed in June 1994. Both concentrated on PC games, combining news, previews and reviews with articles about hardware, modifications and older titles. Reviews used percentage scores, while the surrounding features treated the computer as something readers could change and explore as well as a machine on which to play. Its first issue featured Terry Pratchett, interviewed by Gary Whitta about his books and the forthcoming Discworld adventure.

cards.heading: The games that came with the magazine
cards.text: The British magazine initially included a 3.5-inch floppy disc. From issue eleven, a CD edition called CD Gamer appeared alongside it; its first disc collected the material supplied with the previous ten issues. The package later expanded to two CDs and then DVDs. These discs made demonstrations and other software part of the magazine's appeal. In August 2011, the British edition announced that issue 232 would end the regular disc, replacing it with additional editorial pages and other gifts.

cards.heading: A shared website and a public showcase
cards.text: In 2010, PC Gamer relaunched its website by bringing the British and American online communities together. Writers from both editions contributed to the shared site, alongside its forums. In 2015, PC Gamer and Future began the PC Gaming Show at E3. The magazine's history thus extends from a printed guide with software attached to a website and a showcase where developers could present new PC games.

main.title: Prince of Persia 2: The Shadow and the Flame
main.subtitle: An impostor on the throne
main.summary: Prince of Persia 2: The Shadow and the Flame is the 1993 computer sequel developed and published by Brøderbund, with game design by Jordan Mechner.

cards.heading: An impostor on the throne
cards.text: Prince of Persia 2: The Shadow and the Flame is the 1993 computer sequel developed and published by Brøderbund, with game design by Jordan Mechner. Having won the Princess’s hand, the Prince finds that an impostor has taken his place and that nobody at court recognizes him. His escape through a palace window begins a journey across rooftops, islands, caves and ancient ruins. The game retains the first adventure’s carefully measured running, jumping, climbing and sword fighting, but gives its hero a larger world to discover.

cards.heading: A journey beyond the palace
cards.text: Exploration requires more than a quick sword. Loose floors, pressure plates and dangerous drops make observation and precise movement essential, while the Prince’s shadow form and a magical flame become part of the adventure. The manual explains that separating from his body consumes strength and leaves that body helpless until the two reunite. A later time limit adds urgency without governing the opening stages. Mechner’s 1993 production journal records the collaborative work at Brøderbund, including his construction of temple levels. The score is credited to Jonelle Adkisson. The sequel expands a familiar physical vocabulary into a story about identity, exile and return.

main.title: Mortal Kombat II
main.summary: Mortal Kombat II is a 1993 fighting game developed and published by Midway for arcades.

cards.heading: An arcade sequel reaches home systems
cards.text: Mortal Kombat II is a 1993 fighting game developed and published by Midway for arcades. It was later ported to multiple home systems, including MS-DOS, Amiga, Game Boy, Game Gear, Sega Genesis, 32X, Sega Saturn, Super NES, and PlayStation, by Probe Software (later renamed to Probe Entertainment for some ports of the game) and Sculptured Software, and published by Acclaim Entertainment.

cards.heading: Outworld and new finishing moves
cards.text: Mortal Kombat II is the second main installment in the Mortal Kombat franchise, and a sequel to 1992's Mortal Kombat. It improves the gameplay and expands the mythos of its predecessor while introducing more varied finishing moves (including several Fatalities per character and new finishers, such as Babality and Friendship) and several new characters such as Kitana, Mileena, Kung Lao, the hidden character Noob Saibot, and the series' recurring villain, Shao Kahn. The game's plot continues from the first game, featuring the next Mortal Kombat tournament set in the otherdimensional realm of Outworld, with the Outworld and Earthrealm representatives fighting each other on their way to challenge Shao Kahn.

cards.heading: Commercial success and lasting controversy
cards.text: Mortal Kombat II was released to enormous commercial success and critical acclaim, winning several awards and inspiring numerous clones. However, it was also involved in controversy due to the series' continuous depiction of graphic violence. In the years since its release, Mortal Kombat II has been cited as one of the best games in the series, as well as one of the greatest video games ever made. It was succeeded in 1995 by the direct sequel Mortal Kombat 3, and in 2005 by the spin-off Mortal Kombat: Shaolin Monks, which takes place during the events of Mortal Kombat II.

main.title: NBA Jam
main.summary: NBA Jam is a 1993 basketball video game developed and published by Midway for arcades.

cards.heading: Two-on-two basketball in the arcade
cards.text: NBA Jam is a 1993 basketball video game developed and published by Midway for arcades. It is the first entry in the NBA Jam series and the third basketball video game released by Midway, after TV Basketball (1974) and Arch Rivals (1989). The gameplay of NBA Jam is based on Arch Rivals, being primarily based around a 2-on-2 basketball game.

cards.heading: Midway wins the NBA licence
cards.text: Development followed the financial failure of Midway's Total Carnage (1992). The team sought a wider audience by combining digitized graphics with the two-on-two basketball of Arch Rivals (1989). A licence from the National Basketball Association supplied recognizable teams and players. The association initially questioned Midway's emphasis on arcade action, but the company's executives persuaded it to support the project. Acclaim acquired the publishing rights for home-console versions.

cards.heading: Arcade success reaches home consoles
cards.text: The game was released in arcades in April 1993, with many releases on consoles in the following years. NBA Jam was a critical and commercial success, and it has been cited by critics to be among the greatest video games of all time. The game totaled 6 million units worldwide across SNES and Sega Genesis as of 2019, while the arcade cabinets shipped over 20,000 units as of 2012, totaling over $2 billion in lifetime revenue. Its release was regarded as being highly influential to the sports genre. NBA Jam popularized a subgenre of basketball based around fast action and exaggerated realism which developer Midway eventually applied to other sports in the genre. Several aspects like the implementation of several of its catchphrases also became prevalent in basketball culture in the years following its release.

main.title: Disney's Aladdin
main.subtitle: Virgin’s original Mega Drive adventure, 1993
main.summary: Disney's Aladdin is a 1993 side-scrolling platformer video game developed by Virgin Games and published by Sega for the Genesis. The game is based on the 1992 Walt Disney Animation Studios film of the same name, and features the titular Aladdin navigating settings and scenarios from the film.

cards.heading: Agrabah in motion
cards.text: Disney's Aladdin is a 1993 side-scrolling platformer video game developed by Virgin Games and published by Sega for the Genesis. The game is based on the 1992 Walt Disney Animation Studios film of the same name, and features the titular Aladdin navigating settings and scenarios from the film.

cards.heading: Making room for animation
cards.text: Its animation was the result of a close relationship between drawing and programming. Animation director Mike Dietz recalled how David Perry gave movement unusual priority, while their compression system and Andy Astor’s tools made room for more frames on the cartridge. Expressive sword swings, startled reactions and idle gestures gave the small sprite the personality of a cartoon performer. Aladdin could fight with a scimitar, throw a limited supply of apples and travel from Agrabah to the Cave of Wonders.

cards.heading: The original and its later return
cards.text: The Mega Drive game is distinct from Capcom’s Super Nintendo adaptation of the same film. In 2019, Digital Eclipse brought Virgin’s original back in Disney Classic Games: Aladdin and The Lion King, alongside an explicitly separate Final Cut with camera refinements and other adjustments. The expanded 2021 collection included both 16-bit Aladdin games. These later editions preserve a useful comparison between different ways of translating the same animated story into movement, timing and level design.

main.title: Kid Dracula
main.subtitle: Konami · Game Boy
main.summary: Kid Dracula is Konami's Game Boy platformer about a young vampire trying to recover his castle from Garamoth. He has forgotten most of his abilities, so the journey through eight stages gradually restores the powers needed to overcome its changing obstacles. The character and enemies turn Castlevania's horror imagery into a cartoon comedy, with a pirate ship, factory and volcano among the destinations. The player begins with a straightforward projectile attack, then finds that the familiar-looking hero can answer later hazards in increasingly unusual ways.

cards.heading: A small vampire remembers his powers
cards.text: Kid Dracula is Konami's Game Boy platformer about a young vampire trying to recover his castle from Garamoth. He has forgotten most of his abilities, so the journey through eight stages gradually restores the powers needed to overcome its changing obstacles. The character and enemies turn Castlevania's horror imagery into a cartoon comedy, with a pirate ship, factory and volcano among the destinations. The player begins with a straightforward projectile attack, then finds that the familiar-looking hero can answer later hazards in increasingly unusual ways.

cards.heading: Another ability changes the route
cards.text: Recovered powers expand the form and reach of Kid Dracula's attacks, while others affect movement through the stages. Brief flight, reversed gravity and an umbrella introduce different relationships to an obstacle that would otherwise stop the little vampire. A bomb can damage enemies and remove selected walls. The gradual return of abilities gives the campaign a clear sense of development. The next stage tests what has been learned, then introduces another reason to reconsider what the character can reach or safely pass.

cards.heading: A comic relation of Castlevania
cards.text: The Game Boy release followed Konami's 1990 Famicom Kid Dracula, revisiting parts of its playful world through another portable adventure. Large, clear characters help the jokes remain visible on the small display, while the changing locations give the restored powers different uses. Released in Japan and North America in 1993, it represents another side of the Castlevania family. Its monsters and castle belong to the same broad visual tradition, but the immediate attraction is the expressive young vampire becoming more capable one small discovery at a time.

main.title: Star Fox
main.summary: Star Fox, known as Starwing in PAL regions, is a 1993 rail shooter game developed by Nintendo EAD and Argonaut Software, and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).

cards.heading: Fox and the original squadron
cards.text: Star Fox, known as Starwing in PAL regions, is a 1993 rail shooter game developed by Nintendo EAD and Argonaut Software, and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES). The first entry in the Star Fox series, the story follows pilot Fox McCloud and his elite squadron of mercenaries known as the Star Fox team defending their homeworld of Corneria against the invading forces of the malevolent mad scientist Andross.

cards.heading: Polygons powered by Super FX
cards.text: It was the second 3D Nintendo game after X for the Game Boy in 1992, and the first Nintendo game to use polygonal graphics, achieved with the Super FX graphics chip included in the cartridge. At the time, the complex display of three-dimensional models using polygons was uncommon in console games.

cards.heading: A sequel finally released
cards.text: Regarded as one of the greatest and most influential video games of all time, Star Fox pioneered 3D rail shooter gameplay on home consoles, popularized the use of the Super FX chip, and established the Star Fox series as a flagship Nintendo franchise. The game received critical acclaim, sold more than 4 million copies, and inspired numerous sequels and spin-offs. A sequel, Star Fox 2, was developed but remained unreleased until 2017 as part of the Super NES Classic Edition. The next-released game in the series, Star Fox 64, is a 1997 reboot for the Nintendo 64 and further expanded the series' influence on 3D space combat and squad-based gameplay.

cards.heading: Star Fox returns on Classic Mini
cards.text: The game was re-released worldwide as part of the Super NES Classic Edition in September 2017, and for the Nintendo Classics service in September 2019.

main.title: Lords of Thunder
main.subtitle: A knight flying into heavy metal
main.summary: Lords of Thunder is Red Company's fantasy shooting game, released for TurboDuo in North America in March 1993 and in Japan as Winds of Thunder that April.

cards.heading: A knight flying into heavy metal
cards.text: Lords of Thunder is Red Company's fantasy shooting game, released for TurboDuo in North America in March 1993 and in Japan as Winds of Thunder that April. The armored knight Landis flies through scrolling stages to confront the dark forces threatening Mistral. Elemental armor changes his weapons, while a forceful recorded rock score accompanies the battle. The mixture gives a familiar shooter structure a different personality: the central figure is a flying warrior, and the next choice begins before he enters the stage.

cards.heading: Choose the armor before the battle
cards.text: The first six stages can be tackled in a chosen order. Before each one, the player selects armor associated with an element, changing Landis's shots and bombs. His sword also threatens nearby enemies, rewarding careful proximity as well as distant firing. Large bosses close the stages, while power crystals strengthen the attack along the way. Damage reduces both health and firepower, so surviving a difficult passage concerns the strength available for the next encounter too. Clearing the six routes opens the final stage of the campaign.

cards.heading: Crystals buy another chance
cards.text: Enemies drop colored crystals that serve as money in the shop between stages. The player can buy bombs, protective items and health-restoring supplies, turning a successful run into preparation for another battle. Satoshi Miyashita of T's Music composed the soundtrack, and Masamune Shirow illustrated the cover. The development team included former Technosoft staff with experience on Thunder Force. That background carries into the brisk shooting, while the elemental equipment, shop and hard-rock accompaniment establish the particular character of this CD-based adventure.

main.title: Dragon Ball Z: Super Butōden
main.summary: Dragon Ball Z: Super Butōden, known as Dragon Ball Z in Europe, is a 1993 fighting video game developed by Tose and published by Bandai for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.

cards.heading: Dragon Ball enters the fighting genre
cards.text: Dragon Ball Z: Super Butōden, known as Dragon Ball Z in Europe, is a 1993 fighting video game developed by Tose and published by Bandai for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System. It is based upon Akira Toriyama's Dragon Ball franchise, and was its first fighting game.

cards.heading: Street Fighter inspires the battle system
cards.text: Due to the popularity of Street Fighter II: The World Warrior at the time, producer Toshihiro Suzuki chose to work on a fighting game when assigned to a new project due to it being his preferred genre. Its gameplay consists of one-on-one fights, with a main six-button configuration, featuring special moves, as well as three playable modes.

cards.heading: Success starts a line of sequels
cards.text: Dragon Ball Z: Super Butōden garnered mostly positive reception from critics; most reviewers praised the presentation and gameplay but others felt divided in regards to several design aspects. The game sold approximately 1.3 million units in its first two months of release in Japan. Super Butōden would spawn several sequels; including Dragon Ball Z: Super Butōden 2 (1993), Dragon Ball Z: Super Butōden 3 (1994), Dragon Ball Z: Buyū Retsuden (1994), Dragon Ball Z: Shin Butōden (1995), Dragon Ball Kai: Ultimate Butōden (2011), and Dragon Ball Z: Extreme Butōden (2015).
